ideas.myth: Opposites attract. Birds of a feather flock together.
ideas.takeaway: Which trait would you check first?

sources.cite: Horwitz, T. B., et al. (2023). Evidence of correlations between human partners based on systematic reviews and meta-analyses of 22 traits and UK Biobank analysis of 133 traits. Nature Human Behaviour, 7, 1568-1583.

ideas.replication_check: 2023 study, post-crisis, n=79k UK Biobank — passes

ideas.question_en: Does the bystander effect actually exist?
ideas.hook: You've heard nobody helps when there's a crowd. Cameras say otherwise.
ideas.myth: The more people watching, the less likely anyone helps.
ideas.myth_attribution: Kitty Genovese, 1964. Taught in every intro psych class since.
ideas.data_statement: Nine out of ten times, someone stepped in.
ideas.mechanism: Each person is less likely to act in a crowd, but a crowd has more people who might. The odds per person drop; the odds that someone helps go up.
ideas.verdict: Crowds don't freeze. They just wait.
ideas.verdict_support: The danger isn't that nobody helps. It's that everyone waits for someone else to go first.
ideas.takeaway: Would you be the first to move?

sources.cite: Philpot, R., Liebst, L. S., Levine, M., Bernasco, W., & Lindegaard, M. R. (2020). Would I be helped? Cross-national CCTV footage shows that intervention is the norm in public conflicts. American Psychologist, 75(1), 66-75.
Fischer, P., et al. (2011). The bystander-effect: A meta-analytic review on bystander intervention in dangerous and non-dangerous emergencies. Psychological Bulletin, 137(4), 517-537.

ideas.replication_check: Pasa. El estudio CCTV tiene n=219 conflictos (<500), pero la tesis se ancla en el meta-análisis de Fischer 2011 (7,700 participantes, 105 efectos). Ambos coinciden: el efecto existe por persona, pero no impide que alguien ayude.

ideas.question_en: Why do lies spread faster than the truth?
ideas.hook: It's not the bots. 126,000 stories say it's us.
ideas.myth: Fake news spreads because bots and trolls push it.
ideas.myth_attribution: The default explanation after every viral hoax.
ideas.data_statement: A lie reached 1,500 people six times faster.
ideas.mechanism: False stories were more novel than true ones, and novelty is what makes us share. Bots spread true and false news at the same rate. The difference came from people.
ideas.verdict_support: The truth is usually something you've heard before. A lie almost never is.
ideas.takeaway: What was the last thing you shared because it surprised you?

sources.cite: Vosoughi, S., Roy, D., & Aral, S. (2018). The spread of true and false news online. Science, 359(6380), 1146-1151.

ideas.replication_check: Pasa. Estudio de escala enorme en Science, post-2015, sin controversia sobre el hallazgo central.
ideas.political_note: El paper reporta que el efecto es más fuerte en noticias políticas. El video NO usa ejemplos políticos: el ángulo es novedad + personas vs bots. Si el guion deriva a política, falla el corte de temperatura.

ideas.question_en: Why do siblings raised the same turn out so different?
ideas.hook: Same parents, same house, same rules. Completely different people.
ideas.myth: Kids turn out like the home they grew up in.
ideas.myth_attribution: The assumption behind almost every parenting book.
ideas.mechanism: Siblings share only about half their genes, and the rest comes from experiences each child lives alone: different friends, teachers, accidents. The shared home explains surprisingly little.
ideas.verdict: You didn't grow up in the same house.
ideas.verdict_support: Same address, different childhood. Each sibling lived a version nobody else saw.
ideas.takeaway: What happened to you that your sibling never lived?

sources.cite: Polderman, T. J. C., Benyamin, B., de Leeuw, C. A., Sullivan, P. F., van Bochoven, A., Visscher, P. M., & Posthuma, D. (2015). Meta-analysis of the heritability of human traits based on fifty years of twin studies. Nature Genetics, 47(7), 702-709.

chart_spec.caption: What makes you, you
chart_spec.support_fact: In 69% of traits, sharing a home added nothing measurable.
chart_spec.note: 50 years of twin studies, 14.5 million pairs

ideas.replication_check: Pasa. Meta-análisis de 50 años de estudios de gemelos. 'Nada medible del hogar compartido' se afirma solo para el 69% de rasgos, como dice el paper — no generalizar.

ideas.question_en: Why does time speed up as you age?
ideas.myth: A year is 20% of your life at five. Only 2% at fifty.
ideas.verdict: It's not your age. It's your calendar.
ideas.takeaway: What would you take off this week?

sources.cite: Friedman, W. J., & Janssen, S. M. J. (2010). Aging and the speed of time. Acta Psychologica, 134(2), 130-141.
Janssen, S. M. J., Naka, M., & Friedman, W. J. (2013). Why does life appear to speed up as people get older? Time & Society, 22(2), 274-290.

ideas.replication_check: 2010 + 2013 large-n survey studies, cross-cultural replication (NL, NZ, JP) — passes

sources.cite: Killingsworth, M. A., Kahneman, D., & Mellers, B. (2023). Income and emotional well-being: A conflict resolved. PNAS, 120(10), e2208661120.

ideas.replication_check: Colaboración adversarial post-2015. CONTESTADO: comentarios posteriores en PNAS (Arslan 2024) y un reanálisis en arXiv discuten dónde está el umbral. Usar el acto 4 para decir que sigue en debate.

ideas.question_en: Why does everyone think they drive better than average?
ideas.hook: Ask a room full of drivers. Almost all of them rate themselves above average.
ideas.myth: I'm a safer, more skillful driver than most people on the road.
ideas.data_statement: 91% call themselves more skilled. 93% call themselves safer.
ideas.mechanism: People grade themselves on their best moments at the wheel and everyone else on a vague, generic 'other driver.' Comparing yourself to a blur instead of real data is what lets almost everyone come out ahead.
ideas.verdict: You can't all be above average.
ideas.verdict_support: The average is just where half the drivers you're judging actually are.
ideas.takeaway: Which driver were you rating yourself against?

sources.cite: Svenson, O. (1981). Are we all less risky and more skillful than our fellow drivers? Acta Psychologica, 47(2), 143-148.

Koppel, L., Andersson, D., Tinghög, G., Västfjäll, D., & Feldman, G. (2023). We are all less risky and more skillful than our fellow drivers: Successful replication and extension of Svenson (1981). Meta-Psychology.

ideas.replication_check: Pasa. Koppel et al. 2023 (Meta-Psychology) es una réplica preregistrada de gran n (1,203) que confirma el hallazgo original de Svenson 1981 — el efecto sobrevive la crisis de replicación.

ideas.question_en: Why do intelligent people believe conspiracy theories?
ideas.lead_source: Douglas et al., Annual Review of Psychology, 2019
ideas.reject_reason: Corte de fuente: la cita de la cola (Annual Review of Psychology, 2019) es incorrecta — el paper real es Douglas, Uscinski, Sutton, Cichocka, Nefes, Ang & Deravi (2019), 'Understanding Conspiracy Theories', Political Psychology 40(S1), 3-35 (verificado 2026-09-26). Es una revisión narrativa de múltiples factores psicológicos/políticos/sociales, sin un hallazgo único cuantificable con n≥500 que se pueda graficar en una barra o línea legible en 4s. Falla fuente y graficabilidad.
ideas.note: Fuente ancla identificada, verificada y descartada en la corrida del 2026-09-26.

ideas.question_en: Why do you still remember that embarrassing moment?
ideas.reject_reason: Corte de fuente: el estudio de diario de Rasmussen & Berntsen sobre memorias autobiográficas involuntarias tiene n=14 participantes (verificado 2026-09-26) — muy por debajo del umbral n≥500 / meta-análisis exigido. No se encontró un meta-análisis o estudio de gran escala equivalente centrado específicamente en memorias vergonzosas involuntarias.
ideas.note: Fuente ancla identificada, verificada y descartada en la corrida del 2026-09-26.
